title: Zendesk MCP Server Setup Guide for Claude (2026)
summary: The zendesk mcp server lets you connect Claude to your Zendesk tickets for automated support tasks. Verify you have the prerequisites before setting up.
body_markdown:
## Connect Zendesk to your MCP client


Four steps, and each leaves something working, so you can identify which step broke.


The four are access enabled in Admin Center, a credential that authenticates, a client that lists the server's tools, and one read that returns a real ticket.


The role you authorise as in step 2 is the one the model sees through, so pick it deliberately.


Open Admin Center, go to Apps and integrations, then APIs, then the Zendesk API page. Switch on token access there. If you skip this, **every later call fails with a 401** that looks like a bad credential but is a switched-off feature.


When the toggle is on and saved, the account will accept API requests, which is all this step has to leave you with.


### Step 2: Authorise the connection


On the same page, create an API token and copy it immediately, because Zendesk shows it once. If your server uses OAuth instead, create an OAuth client in the same area and record its client ID and secret.


**Authenticate as a user whose role can see the tickets you care about, not as a full admin by default.** You now hold a credential you can test with a plain HTTP request before any MCP client is involved, and you should.


### Step 3: Add the server to your MCP client


In the client's MCP configuration, add one entry with a name, the command and arguments (or URL) from your server's documentation, and an env block.


Put your Zendesk subdomain, the email of the authorising user and the token in that block, using the variable names the server documents.


Keep the token out of any file you commit. Restart the client fully, since most only read the config at launch. Success is the server appearing in the tool list with its Zendesk tools.


### Test your Zendesk MCP server read-only


Ask the client to list a few recent tickets or fetch one by ID. Don't test with anything that writes. A correct answer means all three layers hold; an empty result usually means the role can't see those tickets.


Afterwards, check that the test touched nothing. An audit log lists each resource, the action taken, who performed it and when, so a read-only test should leave no created, updated or deleted rows.


If the log is clean and the ticket came back, you're done; if not, the fault is in the prerequisites, the permissions or the client config, in that order.
